clue.text: Sect is devious about owning up to fault, mostly expert in wriggling free

indicators.note: a devious route is twisting and indirect, so these letters do not stay in their given order
about here means placed around, so the shuffled letters go round the next piece
mostly means most but not all of the word, so its final letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
to own up to a fault is to apologise

explanation.surface: A shifty religious sect, more or less admitting its errors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Owning up to fault' reads as part of the sect's story, but it is the verb that, cut short, sits inside the jumbled sect.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapologist is a performer, like Houdini, whose act is freeing himself from chains, locks and straitjackets.

clue.text: Very good boom time for developer

blocks.note: so means very, as in 'so kind'
an up is a period of good fortune, as in 'ups and downs'

explanation.surface: A period of high demand that suits a property developer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Developer' makes you think of property, but it is the photographic sense: a chemical bath that brings out the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Soup is old photographers' slang for the chemical developer that brings out the image on film or prints.

clue.text: Dance, one vicar organized with number in Church

indicators.note: to organize something is to put it into a new arrangement, so these letters are reordered
in means placed inside, so the reordered letters sit within the church abbreviation

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England
taken as written, to be rearranged
N stands for a number in algebra

explanation.surface: A vicar arranging a church dance with a number of parishioners.
explanation.definitionFit: The cracovienne is a lively Polish folk dance named after the city of Kraków.

clue.text: Accompanist maybe Bostridge used in track for Winterreise?

indicators.note: something used in another thing is put inside it, so the first name goes within the track

blocks.note: Ian Bostridge is a celebrated English tenor
a piste is a ski track

explanation.surface: Choosing a pianist to accompany Ian Bostridge in Schubert's song cycle Winterreise.
explanation.walkthrough: Bostridge is famous for singing Winterreise ('winter journey'), and a ski piste suits a winter journey. PIANISTE is the French-style form of pianist given in Chambers.
explanation.definitionFit: A pianiste is a pianist, and an accompanist in a song recital is usually one, so 'maybe' marks it as an example.

clue.text: Greedily devourin' what 'ost offers in the main

indicators.note: the dropped aitch in 'ost shows a speaker who leaves off every initial h, so the word is said that way

blocks.note: hogging means eating greedily, here with its final g dropped

explanation.surface: A cockney diner wolfing down whatever the landlord serves.
explanation.walkthrough: The h-dropping speaker of 'ost would say 'oggin' for hoggin'. Oggin is naval slang for the sea, which the old phrase 'the main' also means.
explanation.definitionFit: The oggin is sailors' slang for the sea, and 'the main' is a poetic term for the open ocean.

clue.text: Clyde funnel, individual, not on for dockers

indicators.note: not on tells us to take away those two letters from the word for an individual

blocks.note: lum is the Scots word for a chimney, and the Clyde is a Scottish river
an individual is a person
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: Something about a ship's funnel on the Clyde and a worker who isn't fit for dock work.
explanation.definitionFit: Lumpers are labourers who load and unload ships' cargo, the same job as dockers or stevedores.

clue.text: Part for Gunga Din in historical siege?

indicators.note: a part of a phrase is a run of its letters, so the answer is found inside the name

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words of the name

explanation.surface: Casting someone as Gunga Din, Kipling's water-carrier, in a film about a historic siege.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Siege' is not a military blockade here but its old sense of a seat or throne, as in the Siege Perilous; the question mark signals the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadi is the cushioned throne of an Indian ruler, and siege in its archaic sense means a seat of rank.

clue.text: Sad sound from gnu struggling in the mud?

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
silt is fine mud deposited by water

explanation.surface: A wildebeest stuck in a swamp, letting out a mournful noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A singult is a sob or a hiccup, an old word from Latin singultus, so it is a sad sound.

clue.text: Bream or perch rising around afternoon

around means placed on either side, so the turned word wraps the abbreviation

blocks.note: to perch is to sit
A is short for afternoon, as in p.m. versus a.m. letters

explanation.surface: An angler choosing between bream and perch as the afternoon fish start to rise.
explanation.walkthrough: Bream and perch both look like fish, but perch is the verb sit.
explanation.definitionFit: The tai is a Japanese sea bream, and bream serves as its own plural, matching the plural answer.

clue.text: Old coin: pure gold, half missing, it's damaged

blocks.note: taken as written
the first half of the word gold
taken as written

clue.text: Hybrid culm sown in garden container

a flowerpot is a garden container

explanation.definitionFit: A plumcot is a fruit tree produced by crossing a plum with an apricot, so it is a hybrid.

clue.text: Hack writer

setter's reading: just the definition, since this is the word solvers write their own clues for

explanation.walkthrough: This was the Azed competition word: the puzzle gives only a definition, and entrants submit their own clues for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers once paid a penny per line produced cheap copy in bulk, so the phrase names a low-grade freelance journalist.

clue.text: Exotic party, a humdinger, one replacing start of Lent

start of Lent is its first letter

explanation.surface: A wild party to celebrate before Lent begins.
explanation.walkthrough: The second L of LULU gives way to A.
explanation.definitionFit: A luau is a Hawaiian feast, which counts as an exotic party to most of the world.

clue.text: Port-dweller, one writing off hard-wearing garments

indicators.note: off means taken away, so that abbreviation is removed from the garments

denims are tough cotton work clothes such as jeans
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, a piece of writing

explanation.surface: A docker writing in his tough work clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: An Adeni is a native of Aden, the Yemeni port city, so is a dweller in a port.

clue.text: Short trips round about leg with good extracts from press

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the trips go on either side of what follows

blocks.note: a spin is a short drive or ride
pins is slang for legs
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A quick jaunt involving a leg, with good results from the newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: Snippings are pieces cut out, like press cuttings, so they are extracts from newspapers.

clue.text: Being sullen, pair row, in a muddle

a mess is a muddle

explanation.surface: A couple quarrelling and getting into a state, which leaves them sulking.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a pair is out for nought in both innings, two ducks, hence two Os.
explanation.definitionFit: Moodiness is a tendency to sulk and brood, and being sullen is that same gloomy state as a noun phrase.

clue.text: S-set going up, cast in the wings had a bit of nooky

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means read from the bottom, so these letters are turned round
the wings are the two sides, so the outer word sits on either side of the turned letters

blocks.note: read as soft (P, piano in music) plus set (PUT, as in put down)
a snake casts or sheds its skin

explanation.surface: Backstage at a play: while the scenery goes up, members of the cast are up to mischief in the wings.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'S-' of 'S-set' as printed seems to stand for soft, which crosswords give as P (piano). 'Set', 'cast' and 'wings' all suggest the theatre, but cast is the verb shed.
explanation.definitionFit: Shtup is Yiddish-derived slang for having sex, so shtupped means had a bit of nooky.

clue.text: Puncture's opening on routes becoming rocky or stony

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter
in a down clue on means placed on top, so one piece comes before the other
becoming suggests changing into something new, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the first letter of puncture
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tyre punctured on rough roads that are turning rocky.
explanation.definitionFit: Petrous comes from Latin petra, a rock, and means stony or like rock in hardness.

taken as written, the letters to remove

clue.text: French drivers keep this road badly with it going over earth (7, two words)

taken as written

clue.text: What's on in Paris? It's big in California

clue.text: Nice surprise for traveller, i.e. all's arranged with this in Paris De Gaulle

taken as written, the letters to remove
stands for the answer itself, the letters left over once the others are taken out

explanation.walkthrough: A compound anagram: the letters of I.E. ALL'S together with the answer can be rearranged to spell PARIS DE GAULLE, so removing them leaves the answer's seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An upgrade moves a passenger to a better class of seat at no cost, a welcome surprise on a flight.

clue.text: What a surprise! Cathedral city backing welfare of …

explanation.walkthrough: The dots run on into the next clue: hayle is the welfare of the Poet, meaning Spenser, who used the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Hayle is Spenser's spelling of an old word for welfare or wellbeing, the root of hale and health.

clue.text: … Poet: one kept in food is thrilled

explanation.definitionFit: An odist is a writer of odes, so a poet by trade.

clue.text: Love letter lost in the mail, something from attention-seeker

the post is the mail

clue.text: Layer of quilting, not quite enough for crackers

clue.text: I've got the Queen behind on tow? I'm only joking!
